case_study_insert.main_stem: Northbridge Learning Resources (NLR) is a private limited company in the education publishing sector, employing a workforce of 32. Founded in 2010 by Daniel Okafor, the business produces printed assessment packs for private schools and operates a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership. NLR plans to invest $480,000 in a new digital printing and binding centre with recycled-paper covers, financed by a $280,000 five-year bank loan and $200,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $180,000 a year, a variable cost of $9 a unit and a selling price of $24, and currently produces 20,000 units a year. NLR faces two problems: labour turnover is rising and a growing number of schools report binding defects in delivered packs.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report — Q3 2025: NLR printed 5,200 assessment packs last quarter at a binding-defect rate of 1.9%, down from 3.4% a year ago. Complaints about late deliveries fell from 22 to 9 per month. Average order fulfilment is 2.6 days. A survey of 400 private schools found that 72% would pay up to $1.50 more for packs with recycled-paper covers, and 61% check sustainability when choosing a supplier.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Northbridge Learning Resources for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 3.9% to 4.8%. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.1% from $12.80 to $13.58 per hour from January 2027. (3) Paper and print-input costs have risen 8.4% year-on-year, education supply inflation is 5.5%, and school procurement spending grew 3.1% in the same period.

questions.question_text: NLR is funding part of its $480,000 printing and binding centre with a $280,000 five-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for NLR of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit requires no interest payments or instalments, so the $200,000 contributed internally is cheaper than the $280,000 five-year bank loan. The cash saved can cover the $180,000 a year fixed costs while labour turnover and binding defects in 5,200 packs disrupt production, protecting the $24 selling price from short-term pressure and leaving more of the 720 revenue line as operating profit.

Point 2: Internal funding leaves control with Daniel Okafor and the existing owners, since no lender can impose conditions on the recycled-paper centre or demand security over NLR's assets. With a flat structure and laissez-faire leadership, managers value that autonomy; if school demand falls below the 20,000-unit target there is no loan to reschedule and no risk of repossession, so the business can respond quickly to late-delivery complaints.

Internal funding is especially helpful while binding defects require rework on the 5,200 packs made each quarter, and it avoids the monthly cash outflow that could strain the 2.6-day fulfilment operation.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation applied to NLR and its expansion decision.

questions.question_text: NLR is launching its new recycled-paper assessment packs. Consider a national television campaign, local radio sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should NLR choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Television campaign: A national TV advert could build awareness of recycled-paper packs among schools everywhere, supporting the $480,000 centre. The cost of airtime and production is very high for a 32-employee publisher already committing to a $280,000 loan, and most viewers are not school buyers, so a large share of the budget would be wasted.

Local radio sponsorship: Local radio is inexpensive and can carry a short launch message to schools near NLR, where the 2.6-day fulfilment is strongest. Its drawback is limited reach: packs are supplied to private schools more widely, and local listeners alone cannot create the 20,000-unit volume needed to cover $180,000 fixed costs.

Social media influencer marketing: Education and teacher influencers can show the recycled covers and binding quality directly to school procurement staff, with measurable clicks and low cost per contact. It lets NLR use the survey evidence that 72% of 400 schools would pay $1.50 more for recycled covers and 61% check sustainability, turning Appendix 1 into a targeted message.

Recommendation: NLR should choose social media influencer marketing. It reaches the exact school buyers in the research, is much cheaper than television and wider than local radio, and supports the $1.50 premium needed after the 8.4% rise in paper costs. Television is rejected as unaffordable for a $480,000 expansion, and radio is rejected as too narrow for a publisher targeting 20,000 units a year.

A further advantage is that influencer content can be updated quickly if schools give negative feedback on binding quality, unlike a fixed television slot.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to NLR.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of NLR with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed analysis of all three options in the context of NLR with a justified recommendation explaining why television and radio are rejected.

questions.question_text: NLR has rising labour turnover and schools report binding defects. Explain two benefits for NLR of using laissez-faire leadership to improve motivation in its production team.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Laissez-faire leadership gives experienced packers freedom to decide how to set up the digital presses and binding machines, which can raise intrinsic motivation and job satisfaction. For a 32-employee publisher with a flat structure, that autonomy makes staff feel trusted, and it can reduce the labour turnover that is currently disrupting the 5,200 packs made each quarter.

Point 2: Because workers closest to the machines choose their own methods, they can experiment with ways to cut the 1.9% binding-defect rate and the complaints that fell from 22 to 9 per month. Solving quality problems themselves gives a sense of achievement, and the approach suits a skilled team more than close supervision, helping NLR keep the 2.6-day fulfilment time while the new centre is installed.

Because decisions need not pass through several management levels, a packer can adjust a machine setting as soon as a defect is spotted, keeping the 2.6-day fulfilment promise.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to NLR's turnover, defect rate and delivery performance.

questions.question_text: NLR wants to reduce labour turnover and the 1.9% binding-defect rate. Consider introducing job rotation or offering team-based bonuses. Which should NLR choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Job rotation: Moving staff between printing, binding and packing broadens skills and reduces boredom, which can lower labour turnover and build cover for absent colleagues. It also spreads understanding of where the 1.9% binding-defect rate arises, so workers spot errors earlier. The drawbacks are initial training time and a short dip in output of the 20,000-unit target while people learn each station.

Team-based bonuses: A shared payment linked to fewer defects and on-time dispatch gives a clear collective incentive and could cut the 22-to-9 monthly complaint count further. It is easy to link to the flat structure and laissez-faire culture, but the reward depends on reliable measurement of each pack's quality, and a group payment may let individual carelessness pass unnoticed while still costing NLR cash.

Decision: NLR should introduce job rotation first. It tackles turnover by making work more varied, improves quality understanding across the 32 staff and needs no new cash outlay beyond training, which matters while funding a $480,000 centre. The team bonus is rejected because it requires measurement systems NLR does not yet have and does not address the root cause of repetitive, high-turnover work; it can be introduced later once quality data are consistent.

Cost is also relevant: NLR is already funding a $480,000 centre from a $280,000 loan and retained profit, so a recurring bonus payment would reduce the cash available for new presses. Job rotation uses existing staff and builds a more flexible 32-person team, which is valuable when labour turnover is high. The bonus is therefore rejected on both cost and cultural grounds, since it pays for a result without developing the skills that prevent defects in the first place.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two approaches with limited application to NLR.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both approaches in the context of NLR.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluation of both approaches with a justified decision covering cost, skills and measurement, explaining why the alternative is rejected.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how NLR's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $180,000 ÷ ($24 − $9) = $180,000 ÷ $15 = 12,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 12,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $24 − $9 = $15. Answer: contribution per unit is $15.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways NLR's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 12,000-unit break-even output with 20,000 packs produced: the margin of safety is 8,000 units, showing how far school orders could fall before a loss while labour turnover is rising.
2. Use the $15 contribution per unit to test the $1.50 premium from the survey: raising the $24 price to $25.50 would lift contribution to $16.50, so about 10,909 units would cover $180,000 fixed costs, which informs whether recycled covers can carry a premium.
3. Average total cost is $18 a unit ($180,000 ÷ 20,000 = $9 plus $9) against the $24 price, giving a benchmark for the new digital presses and a floor for bids to private schools.
4. Labour productivity is 625 units per worker (20,000 ÷ 32); tracking it each quarter reveals whether binding defects and turnover are eroding efficiency, and whether the $480,000 centre is delivering its intended gain.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 12,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $15 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 8,000 units against 20,000 units output; pricing test of the $1.50 premium against $180,000 fixed costs; average total cost of $18 against the $24 price; and labour productivity of 625 units per worker to monitor turnover and defects.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate NLR's financial position by calculating the gross profit margin, the profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has NLR's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 45.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 15.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 17.5%
ROCE 2024 = 18.0%
ROCE 2025 = 20.0%

Detailed workings:
2024: revenue 600, cost of sales 360, gross profit 240; 2025: revenue 720, cost of sales 396, gross profit 324. Operating profit rose from 90 to 126 and capital employed from 500 to 630. Interest payable moved from 14 to 18.

Evaluation: Profitability has strengthened on every measure. The trading margin rose from 40.0% to 45.0% because revenue grew faster than cost of sales, so each dollar of school sales keeps more gross profit. The operating margin improved from 15.0% to 17.5%, showing NLR absorbed the $180,000 fixed costs and the binding-defect problem more effectively as the 20,000-unit target was approached. Return on capital edged up from 18.0% to 20.0% despite a larger capital employed figure, which is important before the $480,000 printing centre is added.

Conclusion: NLR's financial position has improved. Higher trading margin, operating margin and return on capital all point in the same direction, so the business is better able to service the $280,000 bank loan. The main caution is that interest payable has risen from 14 to 18 and paper costs by 8.4%, so the margin gains will be tested unless the recycled-cover premium is secured.

The rise in gross profit from 240 to 324 is particularly welcome because it happened while the business still coped with binding defects and late deliveries, suggesting underlying cost control rather than a one-off gain.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the three ratios for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of margin and capital trends and a justified conclusion on whether NLR's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for NLR of introducing recycled-paper covers for its assessment packs.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The survey shows 72% of 400 private schools would pay up to $1.50 more for packs with recycled-paper covers and 61% check sustainability, so NLR can add a premium that lifts the $15 contribution per unit and protects the improved trading margin shown in Appendix 2 against the 8.4% rise in paper and print costs. It also differentiates the packs in a competitive education market and supports the $480,000 centre's positioning.

Disadvantage: Recycled paper can cost more and bind less neatly than standard stock, so the $9 variable cost per unit could rise and eat the $1.50 premium if schools will not pay it. Poorer cover quality could also increase the 1.9% binding-defect rate and the late-delivery complaints, undoing the improvement from 22 to 9 per month just as the new presses are being installed.

NLR should also check that recycled covers survive the binding process and delivery without damage.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to NLR's research, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 4.8%, the 6.1% minimum wage increase to $13.58 and the 8.4% rise in paper and print-input costs will affect NLR. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (3.9% to 4.8%): The increase is 0.9 percentage points, so if the $280,000 five-year bank loan is variable-rate the extra cost is 0.009 × $280,000 = $2,520 a year. This is small against $180,000 fixed costs, and it is zero if the loan was fixed, so NLR can largely neutralise it by fixing the rate. It is not the main threat to the $480,000 centre.

Minimum wage rise (6.1% to $13.58): The insert does not state hours worked or current pay for the 32 staff, so a precise annual wage bill cannot be calculated. The sound judgement is that the whole payroll rises while output must remain near 20,000 units to cover fixed costs; with rising labour turnover, NLR may also face extra recruitment and training expense, so unit labour cost will climb unless productivity of 625 packs per worker is maintained.

Paper and print cost rise (8.4%): As an explicitly labelled upper bound, if the entire $9 variable cost were exposed, 0.084 × $9 = $0.756 per pack, or $15,120 a year at 20,000 units, cutting contribution from $15 to about $14.24. Even a smaller rise matters because it recurs on every pack and competes with the $1.50 premium that 72% of schools might accept.

Conclusion: The 8.4% rise in paper and print-input costs has the greatest impact: it falls on every pack, directly narrows the $15 contribution needed to service the $280,000 loan, and cannot be removed by a simple contract change. The interest rise costs only $2,520 a year and can be fixed, while the wage effect is spread across payroll and uncertain in size, so both are smaller threats.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the three external changes with limited application to NLR.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on NLR's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes with shown derivations from insert figures and a justified greatest-impact judgment with reasons for rejecting the other two.
